arml-2011-power-01b.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-01b.body:
Claim: $\sum_{i=0}^{k}\mathrm{Pa}(n+i,n)=\mathrm{Pa}(n+k+1,n+1)$. Induct on $k$. For $k=0$ both sides equal $1$. If it holds for $k$, add $\mathrm{Pa}(n+k+1,n)$ to both sides: by the recursion,
$$\mathrm{Pa}(n+k+1,n+1)+\mathrm{Pa}(n+k+1,n)=\mathrm{Pa}(n+k+2,n+1),$$
which is the claim for $k+1$. So $m=n+k+1$ and $j=n+1$ (by symmetry $\mathrm{Pa}(m,j)=\mathrm{Pa}(m,m-j)$, so $j=k$ also works). ∎

arml-2011-power-02a.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-02a.body: By definition $\mathrm{Pa}(n,0)=\mathrm{Pa}(n,n)=1$, which is odd, so $\mathrm{PaP}(n,0)=\mathrm{PaP}(n,n)=1$. ∎

arml-2011-power-03a.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-03a.body:
We have
$$\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}=\frac nk\cdot\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!\,((n-1)-(k-1))!}=\frac nk\,\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k-1),$$
so $k\,\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)=n\,\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k-1)$. With $n=2^j$ the right side is divisible by $2^j$, while $0<k<2^j$ means $k$ contains at most $2^{j-1}$ as a power of $2$ (the $2$-adic valuation of $k$ is at most $j-1$). Hence $\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)$ is divisible by $2^{j-(j-1)}=2$, i.e. it is even. Therefore $\mathrm{PaP}(n,k)=0$. ∎

arml-2011-power-03b.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-03b.body:
Work modulo $2$ and induct on $j$. For $j=0$ (so $2^j=1$) the claim $\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)\equiv\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k-1)+\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k)$ is the recursion when $0<k<n$; for $k=0$ or $k=n$ the left side is $1$ and the right side is $0+1$ or $1+0$; for other $k$ all three terms are $0$.

Assume the claim for $j$ and let $n\ge2^{j+1}$. Apply it to $\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)$ and then to each of the two terms (with $n-2^j\ge2^j$):
$$\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)\equiv\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^j,k-2^j)+\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^j,k)$$
$$\equiv\left[\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^{j+1},k-2^{j+1})+\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^{j+1},k-2^j)\right]+\left[\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^{j+1},k-2^j)+\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^{j+1},k)\right].$$
The two middle terms are equal and cancel mod $2$, leaving $\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^{j+1},k-2^{j+1})+\mathrm{Pa}(n-2^{j+1},k)$. ∎

arml-2011-power-05a.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-05a.body:
By 5b below, $\mathrm{Cl}(n,2)=(n-1)^3$, so $\mathrm{Cl}(11,2)=10^3=1000$. (One can also build the triangle row by row.)

**Answer: 1000**

arml-2011-power-05d.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-05d.body:
$\mathrm{Cl}(3,3)=1$ and for $n>3$, $\mathrm{Cl}(n,3)=\mathrm{Cl}(n-1,2)+\mathrm{Cl}(n-1,3)$. Unrolling,
$$\mathrm{Cl}(n,3)=\mathrm{Cl}(n-1,2)+\mathrm{Cl}(n-2,2)+\cdots+\mathrm{Cl}(3,2)+1=(n-2)^3+(n-3)^3+\cdots+2^3+1^3.$$
By the sum-of-cubes identity $1^3+\cdots+m^3=\frac{m^2(m+1)^2}4$ with $m=n-2$: $\mathrm{Cl}(n,3)=\frac{(n-2)^2(n-1)^2}4$. ∎

arml-2011-power-06.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-06.body:
**Claim.** $\mathrm{Cl}(n,k)=6\,\mathrm{Pa}(n,k+1)+\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k-1)$ for $0\le k\le n$, $n\ge1$.

Induct on $n$. *Boundary cases:* for $k=0$ the right side is $6\,\mathrm{Pa}(n,1)+\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,-1)=6n+0=\mathrm{Cl}(n,0)$; for $k=n$ it is $6\cdot0+\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,n-1)=1=\mathrm{Cl}(n,n)$.

*Inductive step:* for $1\le k\le n-1$ (assuming the formula for row $n$),
$$\mathrm{Cl}(n+1,k)=\mathrm{Cl}(n,k-1)+\mathrm{Cl}(n,k)=6\left[\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)+\mathrm{Pa}(n,k+1)\right]+\left[\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k-2)+\mathrm{Pa}(n-1,k-1)\right]$$
$$=6\,\mathrm{Pa}(n+1,k+1)+\mathrm{Pa}(n,k-1),$$
which is the formula for row $n+1$. The boundary entries of row $n+1$ are covered above. ∎

arml-2011-power-07a.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-07a.body:
Use $\mathrm{Le}(n+1,k+1)=\mathrm{Le}(n,k)-\mathrm{Le}(n+1,k)$ starting from $\mathrm{Le}(n+1,0)=\frac1{n+2}$.

Row $4$: $\frac15$; $\frac14-\frac15=\frac1{20}$; $\frac1{12}-\frac1{20}=\frac1{30}$; then by symmetry $\frac1{20},\frac15$.
Row $5$: $\frac16$; $\frac15-\frac16=\frac1{30}$; $\frac1{20}-\frac1{30}=\frac1{60}$; then by symmetry $\frac1{60},\frac1{30},\frac16$.

arml-2011-power-09b.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-09b.body:
By 9c, the infinite sum equals $\mathrm{Le}(m-1,m-1)$, so $n=k=m-1$.

**Answer: $n=k=m-1$**

arml-2011-power-09c.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-09c.body:
The rule gives $\mathrm{Le}(i,m)=\mathrm{Le}(i-1,m-1)-\mathrm{Le}(i,m-1)$. So the partial sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{i=m}^n\mathrm{Le}(i,m)=\mathrm{Le}(m-1,m-1)-\mathrm{Le}(n,m-1).$$
Moreover, $\mathrm{Le}(i-1,j-1)=\mathrm{Le}(i,j-1)+\mathrm{Le}(i,j)>\mathrm{Le}(i,j)$ since all entries are positive, and applying this repeatedly gives $\mathrm{Le}(n,m-1)<\mathrm{Le}(n-m+1,0)=\frac1{n-m+2}\to0$. Thus the infinite sum equals $\mathrm{Le}(m-1,m-1)$, i.e. $n=k=m-1$. ∎

arml-2011-power-10.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-10.body:
Use Leibniz's triangle, where each entry is the sum of the two below it: $\frac13=\mathrm{Le}(2,0)=\mathrm{Le}(3,0)+\mathrm{Le}(3,1)$, and $\mathrm{Le}(3,0)=\mathrm{Le}(4,0)+\mathrm{Le}(4,1)$, $\mathrm{Le}(4,0)=\mathrm{Le}(5,0)+\mathrm{Le}(5,1)$. So
$$\frac13=\mathrm{Le}(5,0)+\mathrm{Le}(5,1)+\mathrm{Le}(4,1)+\mathrm{Le}(3,1)=\frac16+\frac1{30}+\frac1{20}+\frac1{12},$$
giving $\{6,12,20,30\}$. Similarly $\frac13=\mathrm{Le}(4,0)+\mathrm{Le}(5,1)+\mathrm{Le}(5,2)+\mathrm{Le}(3,1)=\frac15+\frac1{30}+\frac1{60}+\frac1{12}$, giving $\{5,12,30,60\}$. And since $\frac1{12}=\mathrm{Le}(12,0)+\mathrm{Le}(12,1)=\frac1{13}+\frac1{156}$,
$$\frac13=\frac15+\frac1{20}+\frac1{13}+\frac1{156},$$
giving $\{5,13,20,156\}$. (Check: $\frac1{6}+\frac1{12}+\frac1{20}+\frac1{30}=\frac{10+5+3+2}{60}=\frac13$, $\frac15+\frac1{12}+\frac1{30}+\frac1{60}=\frac{12+5+2+1}{60}=\frac13$, $\frac15+\frac1{13}+\frac1{20}+\frac1{156}=\frac{156+60+39+5}{780}=\frac13$.)

**Answer: $\{6,12,20,30\}$, $\{5,12,30,60\}$, $\{5,13,20,156\}$**

arml-2011-power-11.title: Solution
arml-2011-power-11.body:
**Claim.** $\mathrm{Le}(n,k)=\dfrac1{(n+1)\,\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)}$ (equivalently $\dfrac{1}{(k+1)\mathrm{Pa}(n+1,k+1)}$).

For $k=0$ and $k=n$, $\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)=1$ and the formula is the definition $\frac1{n+1}$. Induct on $k$ (for all $n>k$ simultaneously): assume the formula for $k$. Then
$$\mathrm{Le}(n+1,k+1)=\mathrm{Le}(n,k)-\mathrm{Le}(n+1,k)=\frac{k!\,(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}-\frac{k!\,(n+1-k)!}{(n+2)!}=\frac{k!\,(n-k)!}{(n+2)!}\left[(n+2)-(n+1-k)\right]$$
$$=\frac{(k+1)!\,(n-k)!}{(n+2)!}=\frac1{(n+2)\,\mathrm{Pa}(n+1,k+1)},$$
using $(n+1)\,\mathrm{Pa}(n,k)=\frac{(n+1)!}{k!(n-k)!}$ and $\frac{(k+1)!(n-k)!}{(n+2)!}=\frac{1}{(n+2)\binom{n+1}{k+1}}$. This is the formula for $(n+1,k+1)$. ∎
